newsitem.title: UK: Scot to sue in England for Namibian injury.
newsitem.headline: Scot to sue in England for Namibian injury.

text.p: Britain's House of Lords ruled on Thursday that a Scotsman could sue Anglo-Australian mining group Rio Tinto Zinc in England for compensation for a cancer he says was caused by working in a Namibian mine.
The decision, which overturned an earlier court ruling, could pave the way for other workers at the Rossing open cast uranium mine, a RTZ subsidiary, to seek damages in England.

Eddie Connelly, 47, says his cancer was caused by years of exposure to high levels of radioactive uranium and silica dust while he worked at the mine from 1977 to 1982. His larynx was removed in 1986.
"The decision could affect a lot of people," his lawyer Clare Hodgson told Reuters.
"The mine is still operating and there have been other people diagnosed with uranium-related diseases," she added.
Connelly was unable to claim compensation from Rossing and he had no way of funding a case in Namibia.
In England he may get state legal aid. Lawyers have said they might take the case on a no-win no-fee basis.
After the case began in England in October 1994, RTZ applied for it to be stayed (halted), arguing that it should be heard in Namibia.
"This a a clear example of an English parent company trying to avoid its responsibilities for dangerous processes carried out abroad," said Richard Meeran, who is also representing Connelly.
"This is a salutary lesson for multinational companies which try to exploit lower health and safety standards in developing countries," he added.
A spokesman for RTZ said the company was very disappointed about the ruling by the House of Lords, England's highest court. It said it still believed the case should be heard in Namibia.

"The decision is about where the case should be heard rather than its merits," said Peter Darling. "Whilst we have every sympathy with Mr Connelly, we believe it (his illness) has absolutely nothing to do with his employment in Namibia."
RTZ also said that health and safety was of primary importance to the company and that experts had inspected the mine and found it to be safe.
Hodgson said she hoped the case will be heard within two years.
